resolved_by: The Sentencing Commission's adoption of USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6), which the dissent describes as resolving the pre-amendment circuit split.
issue: Can a nonretroactive change in federal law be an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' justifying a sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute?

sides.position: Nonretroactive changes in law can, on the face of the statute, be extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction.
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCoy, 981 F.3d 271 (4th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Chen, 48 F.4th 1092 (9th Cir. 2022)
United States v. McGee, 992 F.3d 1035 (10th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Orta, No. 24-5182 (6th Cir. 2025) (dissent)

sides.position: Nonretroactive changes in law cannot, on the face of the statute, be extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction.
cases: United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)

this_court: does not decide. The dissent argues the statute is ambiguous and does not unambiguously foreclose the reading in USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6), which would allow nonretroactive changes to count.
quote: Prior to the Commission’s adoption of USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6), there was a deep circuit split on whether “extraordinary and compelling reasons” could encompass nonretroactive changes in law and, if so, which ones.
cite: United States v. Lois Jochinto Orta, No. 24-5182 (6th Cir. 2025)
